paragraphs: Sequence models must turn their predictions into an output sequence, and beam search is one way to perform that decoding. This paper introduces a fully differentiable beam search decoder. Its central contribution is to let training signals pass through the inference procedure, making decoding part of the computation that can be optimized during training.

This allows models operating at different levels of detail to be trained together. In speech recognition, an acoustic model and a word-level language model contribute different kinds of information. The decoder also supports cases where input and output sequences are not aligned, by considering all possible alignments between them.

The authors demonstrate scalability through an end-to-end speech recognition system trained from word-level transcriptions. Gradients flow through the complete architecture, jointly training the acoustic model and an explicit language model, which may already be pretrained. The result establishes a way to integrate that explicit language model into discriminative training, alongside approaches that learn language structure implicitly.
icml-2019-a-fully-differentiable-beam-se.tldr: A differentiable beam search decoder enables joint training of acoustic and explicit language models through the decoding procedure.

paragraphs: Training a deep network involves optimizing a highly nonconvex function built from nested layers. Backpropagation is the usual approach, but the paper motivates alternatives through issues including vanishing or exploding gradients, nondifferentiable nonlinearities, and difficulties updating layers in parallel. Auxiliary-variable methods offer another formulation by breaking the nested training objective into local subproblems.

The obstacle addressed here is that existing auxiliary-variable approaches mainly operate in batch settings. That limits their usefulness when datasets are extremely large or learning must proceed through incoming observations. The authors introduce an online alternating minimization approach that can train using stochastic updates or minibatches, bringing this alternative formulation into a more incremental learning setting.

The paper contributes what it describes as the first theoretical convergence guarantees for alternating minimization in stochastic settings. It also reports promising results across multiple architectures and datasets. Together, these contributions give theoretical and empirical support for an online alternative to backpropagation, without establishing that it universally resolves every difficulty motivating the work.
icml-2019-beyond-backprop-online-alterna.tldr: An online alternating minimization method extends auxiliary-variable neural-network training to stochastic and minibatch settings with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness asks whether a classifier's predictions remain reliable when its input is deliberately perturbed. This paper studies randomized smoothing, which transforms a classifier that performs well under Gaussian noise into a classifier with provable robustness against perturbations measured by the L2 norm. The quality of the underlying classifier under noise is central to this construction.

The main theoretical contribution is a tight analysis of smoothing, establishing a close relationship between Gaussian noise and L2 robustness. This matters because a certificate provides a guarantee within a specified perturbation size, giving a stronger kind of evidence than performance against a particular collection of attacks.

The authors train an ImageNet classifier with a reported certified top-1 accuracy of 49% for perturbations with L2 norm below 0.5. They also report higher certified accuracies on smaller datasets where competing certification approaches are feasible. These results support prediction-time randomization as a promising route to scalable certified robustness, with the guarantees specifically tied to the stated perturbation norm and radius.
icml-2019-certified-adversarial-robustne.tldr: A tight analysis of randomized smoothing turns Gaussian-noise classification performance into scalable certificates of L2 adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Model-free reinforcement learning can produce substantially different results across runs with different initializations or random seeds. This paper addresses that variability in continuous control by encouraging a learned policy to behave similarly to a policy prior. The regularization acts on the policy's behavior, described as function-space regularization, rather than merely constraining its numerical parameters.

The authors show that this introduces a bias-variance trade-off. Guidance from the prior can reduce variability, while also influencing which behavior the learner favors. They propose an adaptive tuning strategy to manage that trade-off as learning proceeds, making the strength of the prior's influence part of the learning approach.

The stability result has a specific condition: when the prior policy has control-theoretic stability guarantees, regularization approximately preserves those guarantees throughout learning. Across their empirical settings, the authors report significantly lower variance and more efficient learning than deep reinforcement learning alone, alongside dynamic stability. The contribution therefore connects reproducibility of learning outcomes with prior control knowledge, while retaining the stated qualification on stability preservation.
icml-2019-control-regularization-for-red.tldr: Regularizing learned control policies toward a prior reduces performance variability and can approximately preserve the prior's stability guarantees.

paragraphs: An autonomous agent in an open-ended environment must decide what to practice as well as how to act. Some goals may already be easy, while others may be impossible. CURIOUS addresses this allocation problem by building a learning curriculum around progress, with the aim of improving overall mastery across goals that the agent can learn.

The algorithm combines a modular Universal Value Function Approximator with hindsight learning so that one policy can pursue different kinds of goals. Its curriculum mechanism directs attention toward goals with the greatest absolute learning progress. Because the criterion uses absolute change, it can also return attention to abilities that are being forgotten.

Experiments in a new robotic environment with modular goals show a curriculum organizing itself over time. Agents move through goals of increasing complexity and revisit goals when needed. The reported results also demonstrate robustness to distracting goals, forgetting, and changes in body properties. These findings support using measured progress to coordinate exploration and maintenance of multiple skills within one learning system.
icml-2019-curious-intrinsically-motivate.tldr: CURIOUS uses absolute learning progress to organize practice across diverse goals and revisit skills that are being forgotten.

paragraphs: Tukey regression uses a loss that grows approximately as a power of the residual for smaller errors, then becomes constant beyond a chosen threshold. Thus, making an already large residual even larger does not keep increasing its contribution. This paper introduces dimensionality reduction methods for overconstrained regression problems using this loss.

The key mathematical result concerns a fixed low-dimensional subspace. The authors construct a bounded-size set of coordinates that contains all coordinates considered large under the Tukey loss for every vector in that subspace. This shared structural property supports reducing the original regression task to a smaller, weighted problem while preserving a provably good approximation.

The reductions are described as fast and simple, and experiments demonstrate their practicality when existing heuristic solvers handle the smaller problems. The paper separately provides exponential-time algorithms with provable solution quality. Its hardness results suggest that substantially faster worst-case algorithms are unlikely. The practical contribution is therefore a smaller problem with approximation guarantees, alongside a theoretical account of the remaining computational difficulty.
icml-2019-dimensionality-reduction-for-t.tldr: Tukey regression can be reduced to smaller weighted problems with approximation guarantees using a new structural property of subspaces.

paragraphs: Beam search keeps multiple possible output sequences under consideration, allowing choices that a greedy decoder would discard. Increasing its width can find sequences with higher model probability, yet earlier work observed that output quality can deteriorate. This paper investigates that mismatch empirically across three sequence synthesis tasks.

The authors find that wider beams disproportionately select sequences beginning with very low-probability tokens and continuing with tokens that have higher conditional probability. Such sequences can score well under the model overall. In the experiments, however, they are more likely to receive lower evaluation scores than lower-probability sequences without this pattern.

Using the concept of search discrepancies, the authors hypothesize that large departures from locally preferred choices explain the degradation. They argue that this account generalizes earlier explanations from machine translation and image captioning. Constraining beam search to avoid large discrepancies eliminates degradation in their empirical validation. The findings connect a specific search behavior to the observed quality problem while preserving the explanation's status as an empirically supported hypothesis.
icml-2019-empirical-analysis-of-beam-sea.tldr: An empirical study links wide-beam quality degradation to large search discrepancies and shows that constraining them eliminates the observed degradation.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that transformations of an input produce corresponding transformations inside the model. This paper extends that design principle from global symmetries to local gauge transformations. The resulting framework supports convolutional networks on manifolds whose behavior depends on intrinsic geometry, encompassing many existing approaches in equivariant and geometric deep learning.

For a practical implementation, the authors place signals on the surface of an icosahedron, which approximates a sphere. Its regular structure allows the gauge-equivariant convolution to be implemented with a single conv2d call. This connects a general geometric construction to a standard computational operation, making the architecture scalable and practical.

The authors apply the method to segmentation of omnidirectional images and global climate patterns, reporting substantial improvements over previous methods. These tasks demonstrate the usefulness of the construction for signals distributed over approximately spherical surfaces. The paper's contribution combines a broad architectural framework with a concrete implementation that makes its geometric principles computationally accessible.
icml-2019-gauge-equivariant-convolutiona.tldr: Gauge equivariance provides a general framework for geometric CNNs and an efficient icosahedral implementation with improved segmentation results.

paragraphs: The paper considers objectives made from a sum of smooth functions plus a convex term that may be nonsmooth. The complete objective can still be nonconvex. Existing variance-reduction methods address these problems either by occasionally computing a full gradient or by keeping a collection of individual stochastic gradients in memory.

Katalyst builds on Katyusha, an SVRG-type method originally developed for convex optimization. Its target is the regime where the nonconvex objective is close to convex, expressed through a large condition number in the paper's formulation. The proposed adaptation improves the complexity of solving these problems while retaining the SVRG-type approach, which can require less memory than SAGA-type methods.

The authors state that, to their knowledge, the resulting complexity has the best dependence on both the number of component functions and the degree of nonconvexity. It also matches a recent accelerated SAGA-type result for a constrained smooth problem. The significance is a sharper computational guarantee in this particular near-convex regime, achieved through an adaptation of an existing convex optimizer.
icml-2019-katalyst-boosting-convex-katay.tldr: Katalyst adapts convex Katyusha to improve optimization complexity for nonconvex objectives that are close to convex.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to control a linear-quadratic system when its dynamics are unknown. The learner therefore has to choose control actions without already having a complete description of how the system responds. The contribution concerns both the accumulated cost of learning and the computational efficiency of the algorithm used to make those decisions.

The authors present an algorithm with regret bounded at the square-root scale in the time horizon T, with logarithmic factors suppressed by the stated notation. Regret measures accumulated excess cost relative to a comparison controller. A square-root dependence means this excess grows more slowly than the horizon itself, so the corresponding bound on excess cost per step decreases as the horizon grows.

The central achievement is obtaining that regret guarantee with a computationally efficient algorithm for unknown dynamics. The authors identify this combination as a first result and as resolving an existing open question. The stated finding is thus a theoretical advance joining learning performance and tractable computation in linear-quadratic control.
icml-2019-learning-linear-quadratic-regu.tldr: The paper gives a computationally efficient algorithm with square-root regret, up to logarithmic factors, for linear-quadratic control with unknown dynamics.

paragraphs: Training a neural summarizer usually requires documents paired with example summaries, but such datasets are scarce and can transfer poorly between domains. MeanSum tackles a setting containing only product or business reviews, with no summaries supplied for training. Its aim is to generate a new summary from several reviews rather than simply select passages from them.

The model uses an autoencoder and averages the representations of the input reviews. That mean representation is decoded into a summary-review. This makes averaging in the representation space the central mechanism for combining documents within an end-to-end neural architecture. The authors investigate architectural variants and use an ablation study to assess the importance of individual components.

Metrics and human evaluations indicate that the generated summaries are fluent, relevant, highly abstractive, and representative of the reviews' average sentiment. The authors also collect a reference evaluation dataset and report outperforming a strong extractive baseline. These findings support learning multi-review summarization from documents alone, with evaluation summaries used to assess the resulting system.
icml-2019-meansum-a-neural-model-for-uns.tldr: MeanSum generates review summaries without training summaries by decoding the average of input-review representations.

paragraphs: Generating related data across several domains requires modeling how those domains fit together. Methods that work well for two domains can become difficult to scale as more domains are added. This paper introduces MMI-ALI, a deep generative model designed to match a joint distribution across an arbitrary number m of domains.

The approach assembles adversarially learned inference models and trains them using multivariate mutual information. This information objective involves the variables from each pair of domains together with their shared feature. The authors derive feasible losses that upper-bound negative multivariate mutual information and prove their connection to matching the joint distribution across all m domains.

The model scales linearly with the number of domains, addressing the computational growth that motivates the work. Evaluations across diverse multidomain scenarios report superior performance. The contribution combines a scalable model structure with a theoretical link from trainable objectives to joint distribution matching, giving pairwise components a role in a broader multidomain learning objective.
icml-2019-multivariate-information-adver.tldr: MMI-ALI combines adversarial inference models and multivariate-information objectives to match multidomain joint distributions with linear scaling in domain count.

paragraphs: Communication systems need to compress information and protect it against transmission noise. Classical information theory supports separating these jobs in an asymptotic setting. This paper focuses on finite bit lengths and limited computation, where separate coding schemes can require substantial tuning and decoding can be costly.

The authors jointly learn encoding and decoding with a discrete variational autoencoder. During training, noise is added to the latent codes to simulate the communication channel. This exposes the model to transmission errors while it learns a representation, allowing compression and error correction to be shaped together under fixed bit-length and computational budgets.

The learned codes are competitive with several separation schemes and also provide robust representations useful for downstream classification. The neural decoder uses amortized inference, replacing repeated decoding work with a learned inference procedure. The authors report decoding almost an order of magnitude faster than standard iterative belief-propagation methods. The results support joint learning as a practical option when transmission length and decoding resources are constrained.
icml-2019-neural-joint-source-channel-co.tldr: A discrete variational autoencoder jointly learns compression and error correction under fixed budgets, producing competitive codes and fast neural decoding.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering vectors when quality is measured using entropy or Gini impurity. The focus is on how well an algorithm can approximate the best clustering and what computational barriers prevent stronger guarantees. Its main stated theoretical advances concern clustering under entropy impurity.

The authors provide the first polynomial-time algorithm for this objective whose approximation guarantee does not depend on the number of vectors. That separates the guarantee's quality from the dataset's size. They also establish that entropy-impurity clustering does not admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme, placing a theoretical restriction on the possibility of increasingly accurate polynomial-time approximations.

The hardness result also resolves an open question about information-theoretic clustering of probability distributions. Beyond these guarantees and barriers, the authors develop a clustering method from the same theoretical tools and test it experimentally. The experiments suggest practical usefulness, particularly when many clusters are required. The paper therefore connects approximation theory with an empirically promising method while keeping its practical conclusions appropriately tentative.
icml-2019-new-results-on-information-the.tldr: The paper improves entropy-clustering approximation guarantees, establishes an approximation barrier, and develops an empirically promising clustering method.

paragraphs: Median-of-means learning compares candidate decision rules across blocks of training data. A rule wins a comparison when it performs better on most blocks, giving a tournament-style alternative to choosing the best overall empirical average. Prior results motivate this approach through robustness and strong mean-squared-error performance under minimal assumptions in nonparametric regression.

This paper extends the framework in two directions. First, blocks can be formed through independent sampling without replacement rather than a single segmentation of the dataset. The authors prove that the existing median-of-means bounds are essentially preserved under this randomized construction, broadening the ways data can be organized for comparisons.

Second, the analysis extends to objectives defined over pairs of observations, whose empirical forms are U-statistics. Such objectives arise in ranking, clustering, and metric learning. This makes the tournament approach relevant beyond losses attached to individual examples. The paper supplies theoretical performance guarantees for the proposed learning and estimation methods, with numerical experiments providing additional evidence of practical relevance.
icml-2019-on-medians-of-randomized-pairw.tldr: Median-of-means guarantees largely survive randomized block construction and extend to learning objectives based on pairs of observations.

paragraphs: PicCoLO is a framework for accelerating policy learning by adding predictive models to existing first-order model-free reinforcement or imitation learning algorithms. It uses a model to anticipate useful updates while retaining feedback from interaction with the environment. The method repeatedly separates learning into a prediction step and a correction step.

During prediction, the model estimates a future gradient that has not yet been observed, and the learner updates its policy using that estimate. It then runs the updated policy in the environment, receives the true gradient, and corrects using the prediction error. The authors explain that this correction removes the model bias arising from imperfect predicted gradients.

The theoretical construction reduces predictable online learning to adversarial online learning. This supplies a systematic way to adapt first-order algorithms and achieve optimal regret relative to the available predictable information. Theory and simulations show improved convergence rates for several model-free algorithms. The contribution is thus a reusable mechanism for obtaining benefits from predictions while explicitly correcting their mistakes.
icml-2019-predictor-corrector-policy-opt.tldr: PicCoLO accelerates policy learning with predicted gradients and corrects their errors using environmental feedback to avoid model bias.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical view of several machine-learning problems by treating probability distributions as the objects being optimized. The objective is a functional: a quantity that assigns a value to an entire probability measure. Learning is then framed as reducing that value over the space of possible measures.

The authors show that generative adversarial networks, variational inference, and actor-critic reinforcement learning can all be expressed within this framework. These areas are usually presented through their own objectives and algorithms. Bringing them into one formulation makes their shared optimization structure explicit and provides a common language for examining how their methods operate.

The paper introduces a generic optimization algorithm called probability functional descent and shows that it recovers existing methods developed independently in those settings. Its stated contribution is therefore a unifying interpretation together with an algorithmic framework. Recovering those methods demonstrates that the formulation connects to established procedures, beyond merely grouping several applications under a broad conceptual description.
icml-2019-probability-functional-descent.tldr: Probability functional descent unifies GANs, variational inference, and actor-critic methods as optimization over probability measures.

paragraphs: An agent can perform well in environments it has practiced without handling unfamiliar environments equally well. This paper examines that distinction in deep reinforcement learning. It argues that using the same environments for training and testing, as common benchmarks often do, reveals relatively little about generalization.

The authors use procedural generation to create separate training and test environments and introduce CoinRun as a benchmark for this purpose. Separating the two sets makes it possible to assess performance beyond the environments encountered during learning. In CoinRun, the authors find that agents can overfit even when the training set is surprisingly large.

The study also identifies changes that improve generalization in its experiments. Deeper convolutional architectures help, as do L2 regularization, dropout, data augmentation, and batch normalization, all familiar from supervised learning. The findings make generalization a measurable concern within reinforcement-learning evaluation and show that both architectural choices and training techniques can improve performance on held-out environments.
icml-2019-quantifying-generalization-in-.tldr: CoinRun exposes reinforcement-learning overfitting on large training sets and shows that deeper networks and familiar regularization methods improve generalization.

paragraphs: Factorization machines model pairwise feature interactions through low-rank representations. Existing approaches use the same rank for every feature, imposing a uniform representation size. This paper introduces Rank-Aware Factorization Machines, or RaFM, which allow pairwise interactions to draw on embeddings with different ranks.

That flexibility is particularly relevant to datasets where features occur at substantially different frequencies. The authors report improved performance on real-world datasets with this property. The approach changes how representation capacity is organized across feature interactions, allowing the model to move beyond a single fixed rank shared throughout the feature set.

The paper also proves that storing, evaluating, and training RaFM can be as efficient as doing so for one ordinary factorization machine. Under certain conditions, it can be significantly more efficient. Reported improvements cover both regression and classification while reducing computational burden. These results suggest industrial potential because the additional modeling flexibility comes with efficiency guarantees, although the stronger efficiency advantage depends on the stated conditional setting.
icml-2019-rafm-rank-aware-factorization-.tldr: RaFM uses embeddings of different ranks to improve feature-interaction modeling while retaining, and conditionally improving, factorization-machine efficiency.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of vertices, making them useful for modeling higher-order data structure. This paper studies hypergraphs in which a vertex can have a different weight in each hyperedge containing it. Those weights express how much the vertex contributes to each particular group relationship.

The authors use random walks to build a spectral theory for this setting. They derive a hypergraph Laplacian and bound the time required for the walks to mix. They also identify conditions under which these hypergraph walks are equivalent to walks on ordinary graphs, clarifying when a seemingly richer representation changes the underlying computation.

A consequence is that existing methods using random-walk Laplacians with edge-independent vertex weights do not exploit higher-order relationships. This conclusion concerns that specific class of methods. Experiments on real-world ranking applications demonstrate advantages of edge-dependent weights. The work therefore combines mathematical tools for richer hypergraph models with a diagnosis of when hypergraph-based methods effectively reduce to graph-based ones.
icml-2019-random-walks-on-hypergraphs-wi.tldr: Edge-dependent vertex weights support richer hypergraph random walks, while the analysis identifies cases where hypergraph methods reduce to ordinary graph walks.

paragraphs: Decision trees can also be vulnerable to adversarial examples: changes to input features chosen to undermine a model's predictions. This paper demonstrates that vulnerability and develops a training approach intended to improve robustness. Its central idea is to choose tree behavior according to performance under worst-case feature perturbations.

This turns tree construction into a max-min saddle-point problem, combining the learner's choices with an opposing choice of perturbations. Trees make discrete split decisions, and a direct search for the best robust split would require exponential time. The authors make the procedure practical by approximating the inner minimization, reducing the computational obstacle to using the robust objective.

They provide efficient implementations for both classical information-gain trees and boosted tree systems such as XGBoost. Experiments on real-world datasets show significant improvements in adversarial robustness. The result extends robustness-oriented training to widely used tree models and demonstrates that approximating the difficult inner problem can yield useful empirical gains within scalable tree-building procedures.
icml-2019-robust-decision-trees-against-.tldr: Approximate worst-case split optimization makes adversarially robust training practical for decision trees and boosted tree systems.

paragraphs: Standard Metropolis-Hastings sampling commonly requires work proportional to the dataset size at every step, making large-scale Bayesian inference expensive. Scalable Metropolis-Hastings addresses that cost while keeping the true posterior as its invariant distribution. Here, exactness refers to the distribution preserved by the sampling process.

The method combines factorized acceptance probabilities, fast simulation of Bernoulli processes, and control-variate ideas. The authors report that it needs to process only a constant number of data points per step on average, or even a quantity scaling as the inverse square root of dataset size. These are average data-processing claims, allowing some steps to require no data-point processing.

The paper analyzes performance theoretically and gives realistic, verifiable conditions for geometric ergodicity, a property governing convergence toward the invariant distribution. Experiments support overall performance benefits relative to standard Metropolis-Hastings and several subsampling approaches. The contribution shows how substantial reductions in per-step data access can coexist with preserving the exact posterior, with convergence properties established under stated conditions.
icml-2019-scalable-metropolis-hastings-f.tldr: Scalable Metropolis-Hastings sharply reduces average per-step data processing while preserving the true posterior as its invariant distribution.

paragraphs: Causal conclusions depend on assumptions about how data were generated, and some of those assumptions cannot be verified from observations alone. This paper develops a systematic way to ask how a conclusion changes when uncertain assumptions are violated. Its scope is arbitrary linear structural causal models.

The authors formulate sensitivity analysis as a constrained identification problem and introduce an efficient graph-based algorithm. The algorithm uses nonzero constraints on directed and bidirected edges. Researchers can select path coefficients and error covariances as sensitivity parameters, allowing the analysis to represent uncertainty about different aspects of the causal model.

The resulting sensitivity curves show how a target causal quantity changes as those parameters vary. This makes the consequences of assumption violations explicit and helps identify violations large enough to alter a substantive conclusion. Researchers can then use scientific knowledge to judge whether those violations are plausible. The contribution broadens algorithmic sensitivity analysis beyond methods tailored to particular model structures, while retaining the linear-model setting.
icml-2019-sensitivity-analysis-of-linear.tldr: A graph-based framework derives sensitivity curves showing how causal quantities in linear structural models respond to assumption violations.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo methods use samples to approximate quantities that are difficult to compute directly. In vector-space applications, arranging samples to be mutually orthogonal has been shown to improve many machine-learning methods. Enforcing that relationship exactly can be computationally expensive, motivating approaches that approximate it more cheaply.

This paper organizes many approximate orthogonal sampling methods through a common framework based on Givens transformations. The framework provides a shared way to understand methods that might otherwise appear separate. The authors also use it to construct new approximate methods, so the unification contributes both an interpretation of existing techniques and additional algorithmic choices.

For families of approximate methods used in kernel approximation, the authors provide what they describe as the first statistical guarantees. This adds theoretical support in a setting where approximate orthogonality is used to reduce computational demands. Extensive empirical evaluations complement the theory and provide practical guidance, connecting the common framework to decisions about which approximate method to use.
icml-2019-unifying-orthogonal-monte-carl.tldr: A Givens-transformation framework unifies approximate orthogonal Monte Carlo methods, generates new ones, and supplies statistical guarantees for kernel approximation.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a data matrix contains a rank-one signal in addition to noise. It studies a low signal-to-noise regime below the threshold for reliable detection. The goal in this regime is to construct a useful hypothesis test with controlled error, even though reliable detection is unavailable.

The proposed test uses linear spectral statistics, which summarize information from the matrix's spectrum. It is data-driven and does not require the distribution of either the signal or the noise. When the noise is Gaussian, its error matches that of the likelihood-ratio test that minimizes the sum of false-positive and false-negative probabilities.

That optimality claim is specifically for Gaussian noise and the stated combined error criterion. The authors also show that knowing the noise density permits an entrywise transformation that further lowers test error. The result distinguishes what can be achieved without distributional knowledge from the additional benefit available when information about the noise is supplied.
icml-2019-weak-detection-of-signal-in-th.tldr: A spectral test detects weak rank-one signals with optimal combined error under Gaussian noise and can improve further when the noise density is known.
